planting.note: Divide and transplant established clumps in early fall or early spring into humusy, well-drained woodland soil.

directions: This compact European woodland sedge forms neat tufts of narrow, dark green, slightly arching leaves and sends up delicate reddish-brown flower spikes on thin stems in early spring before the tree canopy fills in. It prefers humus-rich, free-draining soil in deciduous shade and resents heavy, waterlogged ground. Use it as a fine-textured filler among hellebores, epimediums, and spring ephemerals in a woodland or shaded rock garden setting. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes and rarely becomes aggressive, making it suitable for small-scale underplanting.

planting.note: Transplant divisions in spring into lean, well-drained soil in dappled shade; established plants tolerate some summer dryness.

directions: A low, slowly creeping European sedge native to calcareous woodland edges and open scrub, forming dense mats of fine, soft green foliage that often takes on reddish-bronze tones through autumn and winter. It thrives in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in light woodland shade and handles drier conditions better than many woodland sedges once established. Plant it as a small-scale groundcover or edging in a shaded rock garden, where its fine texture contrasts well with broader-leaved woodland perennials. It is not aggressive and combines readily with spring bulbs that go dormant by summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or spring in rich, moisture-retentive woodland soil under deciduous canopy, where it can spread freely by rhizome.

directions: Native to deciduous forests across central and eastern Europe, this sedge spreads steadily by rhizome to form a soft, continuous carpet of broad, glossy, lightly hairy leaves beneath beech and oak canopy. It favors rich, consistently moist, humus-laden soil in full shade and is valued in naturalistic woodland plantings as a large-scale groundcover alternative to turf or ivy. Its running habit makes it best suited to open woodland floor areas rather than tight borders, where it can be allowed to knit together with other shade perennials. Give it room, since established colonies spread considerably faster than clump-forming woodland sedges.

planting.note: Transplant small divisions in spring into gritty, well-drained soil in a shaded rock garden or woodland edge position.

directions: This diminutive European alpine sedge forms tight, slow-growing tufts of fine, dark green leaves with small claw-like seed clusters that give the species its common name. It is best grown in gritty, sharply drained, calcareous soil in light shade, where it stays neat and compact for years without spreading aggressively. Its small scale suits shaded rock gardens, trough plantings, and the front of a woodland border alongside other miniature shade perennials. It is the straight green species, distinct from the cream-variegated 'Variegata' selection already more common in cultivation.
